root.moves: 1. d4 f5 2. c4 g6 3. Nc3 Nh6

parent.name: Dutch Defense
parent.overview: Black answers 1.d4 with 1...f5, fighting for e4 and avoiding symmetrical play, at the cost of weakening the kingside (the e8-h5 diagonal) and the e6 square. Three set-ups dominate: the Leningrad (...g6, ...Bg7, KID-style, with ...e5 or ...Ne4 and kingside play), the Stonewall (...e6, ...d5, ...c6 with a knight on e4 and a bad light-squared bishop) and the Classical (...e6, ...Be7, ...d6, later ...e5). White usually fianchettoes with g3/Bg2 and c4 and prepares e4 or queenside expansion, or sidesteps theory with the Staunton Gambit (2.e4), Hopton or Korchnoi Attack (h3 and g4). Sources agree it is sound but double-edged, unbalancing and theoretical, played occasionally by Carlsen, Nakamura and Nepomniachtchi but never a main defence to 1.d4.

parent.name: Bird Opening
parent.overview: 1.f4 stakes a claim to e5 and gives White attacking chances at the cost of slightly weakening the kingside (the h4-e1 diagonal). Black's most common reply is 1...d5, which gives a reversed Dutch Defence with White a tempo up, and White chooses between a reversed Leningrad (Nf3, g3, Bg2, O-O), a Stonewall (pawns on d4, e3, f4, with a kingside pawn storm) or a queenside fianchetto to hold e5. Black's sharpest answer is 1...e5, From's Gambit, which is notoriously double-edged and shows the Qh4+ danger. Other replies include 1...Nf6, 1...c5 and 1...b6. White scores below 50% (about 47%), and the opening is rare at the very top, but it is a respectable surprise weapon (Larsen, Bird).

parent.name: Van't Kruijs Opening
parent.overview: 1.e3 opens lines for the f1-bishop and the queen, claims the e4 square lightly and commits to nothing else; it blocks the c1-bishop, so White plans to free that bishop early (b3, or d4 and Nd2/Bd2). It is mainly a transposition device: c4 gives English-type positions, d4 Queen's Pawn structures, b3 Larsen's Opening, and f4 Bird-type set-ups, and 1...e5 2.e4 is a reversed Open Game. Black has maximum freedom and the opening invites him to over-commit in the centre. It is considered passive but sound and gives White no particular advantage; its popularity has declined and strong players use it mainly to reach known structures.

parent.name: Benoni Defense: Old Benoni
parent.overview: Black answers 1.d4 with 1...c5 before committing to ...d5 or ...Nf6; the root is a crossroads. White normally replies 2.d5, gaining space with a wedge, and Black then has to undermine d5 with ...e6, ...e5, ...d6, ...Nf6 or ...b5 so as not to be squeezed. Main branches are 2.d5 e6 (heading for a Modern Benoni structure), 2.d5 d6 3.e4 (the Schmid Benoni, with a King's-Indian-like set-up), and 2.d5 e5 (Czech Benoni, a locked centre with kingside play by f4 and queenside b4 for White). White can also play 2.dxc5, 2.e3 or 2.c3, which tend to transpose to other structures. Sources describe the opening as a long strategic space-versus-counterplay struggle, playable but demanding, rare at top level though used by Alekhine, Kasparov, Torre and Vaganian.

parent.name: Caro-Kann Defense
parent.overview: Black plays ...c6 to support ...d5 and so challenges the e4 pawn with a sound pawn structure, while keeping the light-squared bishop free to come out to f5 or g4 before ...e6 (the French Defence's main drawback, at the cost of a tempo). Black accepts less space early and tends to get a resilient, hard-to-break structure with few weaknesses and good endgame prospects. Play is mostly positional and manoeuvring; it is called more solid and less dynamic than the Sicilian (s1). The Advance (3.e5 Bf5) and Panov-Botvinnik (3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4) lines are more combative, and the Advance became the most popular White try in the 21st century. Main branches: Classical (4...Bf5), Advance, Exchange, Panov, 4...Nf6 lines, Gurgenidze (...g6), Two Knights (2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3) and Fantasy (3.f3). This is a crossroads root after 1...c6; the pawn structures differ by branch.

parent.name: Hungarian Opening
parent.overview: White plays 1.g3 to fianchetto the king's bishop to g2 and hit the long diagonal, deferring any central commitment (s1, s3). It is a flank opening that usually transposes: into the King's Indian Attack (Nf3, d3, O-O, then e4), the Catalan, the Réti or the English, depending on Black's set-up (s1, s3, s4). Black can happily occupy the centre with ...d5 or ...e5, or choose Sicilian, Caro-Kann or King's Indian-style set-ups (s2, s3). Positions are usually closed or flexible, with long-term strategic play rather than early tactics (s1, s3). Engines and statistics find it essentially equal, with White at most slightly more comfortable (s3, s4). Theory is minimal: it is closer to a move order than a distinct variation (s2).

parent.name: English Opening: Symmetrical Variation
parent.moves: 1. Nf3 Nf6 2. c4 c5 3. Nc3 e6 4. g3 b6 5. Bg2 Bb7 6. O-O Be7
parent.overview: After 1.c4 c5 the opening can stay quiet for several moves and then branch: White chooses between an early d4 break (2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4, or the Anti-Benoni move order), a slow fianchetto set-up (2.g3 or 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 with Bg2, then often Rb1 and b4), or a Maróczy-type bind with e4. Black either mirrors White, plays the double-fianchetto 'ultra-symmetrical' set-up, or adopts a Hedgehog formation. The game is a manoeuvring fight for d5 and d4, rarely forcing in the early middlegame. White tends to want to break the symmetry with d4 to get an unbalanced pawn structure.

parent.name: French Defense: Tarrasch Variation
parent.moves: 1. e4 e6 2. d4 d5 3. Nd2 Nc6
parent.overview: White develops the knight to d2 to protect e4 without allowing the ...Bb4 pin, and keeps the c-pawn free for c3. Black chooses between 3...c5 (immediate challenge to d4, leading to open play and often an isolated d-pawn after 4.exd5 exd5), 3...Nf6 (4.e5 Nfd7 gives a closed French chain where White plays c3, Bd3, Ne2 and sometimes f4, and Black hits the chain with ...c5 and ...f6) and the Rubinstein-style 3...dxe4. Sources describe it as a low-risk, practical weapon for White with less theory than the Classical, aiming for a small, safe edge; Black can equalise with accurate play, especially with 3...c5. The structure type depends entirely on Black's third move: closed and manoeuvring, or open with IQP.

root.name: King's Gambit Declined: Zilbermints Double Countergambit

parent.name: King's Gambit
parent.overview: 2.f4 offers a pawn at once to deflect Black's e-pawn, build a big centre with d4, develop quickly and use the half-open f-file against f7 (Bc4, Nf3, castling). The root covers both the Accepted lines (2...exf4: Kieseritzky 3.Nf3 g5 4.h4 g4 5.Ne5, Muzio, Bishop's Gambit 3.Bc4) and Declined lines (Falkbeer 2...d5, Classical 2...Bc5, and 2...d6 which is the most played move in the database). Accepted lines are sharp and tactically dense; Black tries to hold the pawn with ...g5 or return it with ...d5/...d6 to ease development. Declined lines are more solid and are chosen by stronger players who want to avoid the chaos. Play is open and double-edged for White's king as well.
